newsitem.title: UK: Investors pile into the base metals.
newsitem.headline: Investors pile into the base metals.

text.p: Investment funds boosted London Metal Exchange (LME) base metals prices to new recent highs on Thursday and had traders recalling the heady days of 1993/94.
But otherwise trading in commodity markets was slow and even the base metals eventually gave up some of their recent gains as profittaking set in.

As the speculative interest in metals reached full flow early in the day aluminium prices hit an eight month high of $1,625 a tonne, zinc touched a two year peak of $1,133, tin and nickel both touched four month highs and lead was at its best for two months.

Major investment houses Goldman Sachs and Union Bank of Switzerland pinned their faith in a base metals price boom by issuing base metal warrants, a vehicle pouplar with investors when a big move is looming.
"It could be the return of 1993/94 when they were last issued," said William Adams at brokers Rudolf Wolff recalling the last big bull run in the metals complex.
He noted that in that bull run metal inventories were high and rising but this time their was not quite so much metal around.
Of the setback late in the day Adams said "It's done enough for now and the whole complex needs to pause,"

On the LIFFE coffee market in London prices took an early downturn after news late Wednesday of a rise in stocks of coffee in the U.S. and an end to a dockworkers strike in major coffee exporter Colombia.
But speculators in the U.S. ignored this news and soon reversed the earlier losses and by the end of the day prices were firmly in the plus column.
Brent oil futures on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) paused after Wednesday's sharp rise while gold moved very narrowly during a much quieter day than of late.
